Sea of Glass
SEE uv GLAS
n. phr. (the clear expanse before the throne of God in the Revelation)
English rendering of Greek thalassa hyalinē, a glassy sea, from hyalos, glass or crystal. The figure recalls the molten sea of Solomon's temple and the pavement of sapphire under the God of Israel in Exodus 24:10.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

John sees before the throne “a sea of glass like unto crystal,” and later “a sea of glass mingled with fire.” The sea in Scripture is ordinarily the restless and threatening element, the deep that must be rebuked, the place from which the beast rises. Before the throne it is a sea no longer in motion. It is solid, clear, and still, and the saints stand upon it. That is the whole doctrine of the figure: what is turbulent and hostile in this world is, in the presence of God, floored and transparent. The second vision adds fire to the crystal and sets upon it “them that had gotten the victory over the beast, and over his image, and over his mark, and over the number of his name,” holding “the harps of God.” The fire is the fire of judgment through which they passed, and the glass is the firmness on which they now stand to sing. The temple furniture lies behind the image — the laver of brass in which the priests washed stood between the altar and the holy place, and Solomon's molten sea served the same cleansing office — so that the sea of glass marks the court of a sanctuary where the washing is finished and nothing remains to be cleansed. There is no longer any water to be used, because there is no longer any defilement to remove.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Glass, a hard, brittle, transparent substance. A sea of glass, Revelation 4:6, an expanse clear as crystal before the throne, the figure of a perfect transparency and stillness in the presence of God.

expand to see more

Glass, a hard, brittle, transparent, factitious substance.

Used figuratively of perfect clearness and of that which hides nothing.

A sea of glass like unto crystal, Revelation 4:6, before the throne.

A sea of glass mingled with fire, Revelation 15:2, whereon the victors stand.

Compare the molten sea of the temple, 1 Kings 7:23, and the laver of brass.

Key Scripture

Rev 4:6 — "And before the throne there was a sea of glass like unto crystal: and in the midst of the throne, and round about the throne, were four beasts full of eyes before and behind."

Rev 15:2 — "And I saw as it were a sea of glass mingled with fire: and them that had gotten the victory over the beast, and over his image, and over his mark, and over the number of his name, stand on the sea of glass, having the harps of God."

Exo 24:10 — "And they saw the God of Israel: and there was under his feet as it were a paved work of a sapphire stone, and as it were the body of heaven in his clearness."

Rev 21:18 — "And the building of the wall of it was of jasper: and the city was pure gold, like unto clear glass."

Modern Corruption

The sea of glass is treated as scenic decoration in an exotic vision rather than as the sanctuary figure it is — the chaos of the world made still and the cleansing finished.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What it faces instead is neglect, and a particular kind of neglect: the Revelation's throne-room furniture is read as atmosphere. Commentators and readers alike move quickly past the sea of glass toward the parts of the book that can be turned into a timeline, and in doing so they lose the one detail the figure exists to carry. John is describing a sanctuary. The sea before the throne answers to the laver before the holy place, and the saints standing on it are standing where water used to be needed. That is a statement about the completeness of the cleansing accomplished by Christ, and it is of a piece with the later word that in the city there is no temple and no need of the sun.

The principle to recover is that the images of Revelation are drawn from the tabernacle and the temple, and are read rightly only by a reader who knows that furniture. The sea of glass is not a decorative flourish; it is the still, floored, transparent answer to Genesis 1:2 and to every sea in the Psalms that roars and will not be quiet. Mingled with fire, it says that the saints who stand there came through judgment and were not consumed. The right response to the figure is the response the text itself records — they stand, and they have the harps of God, and they sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek thalassa, a sea; hyalinē, glassy, from hyalos, glass or crystal; a still and transparent expanse before the throne.

expand to see more

Greek thalassa, the sea, in Scripture often the restless and hostile deep.

Greek hyalos, glass, crystal; hyalinē, glassy, transparent.

Like unto crystal, Revelation 4:6, marking perfect clearness.

Mingled with fire, Revelation 15:2, the judgment the victors passed through.

Answers to the laver of brass and the molten sea of the temple.

Usage

"before the throne there was a sea of glass like unto crystal"

"I saw as it were a sea of glass mingled with fire"

"stand on the sea of glass, having the harps of God"
